title: Wedding Videography

jokes.text: Abed explains he can't say who he's working for because 'It's a surprise' — delivered deadpan while filming covertly in a classroom
jokes.setup: Jeff suspects Abed might be a spy for the city, treating it as a serious concern
jokes.punchline: Abed reframes his secrecy not as espionage mystery but as a cute surprise reveal — completely deflating the tension
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Abed — recontextualizing paranoid spy logic into something wholesome and mundane. The deadpan delivery is core to the character and the subversion of Jeff's concern is clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The bar for educational achievement is literally not erasing one word

jokes.text: Jeff says 'You know the rules, Jeff. The sooner you ignore me, the sooner I stop being a factor.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Abed not to get in the way
jokes.punchline: Abed instructs Jeff on how the meta-rules of his own presence work, speaking to Jeff by name as if reading from a show bible
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Abed speaking meta-narratively about his own role in a scene — explaining the rules of his documentary function to the subject of the documentary — is brilliantly self-aware. 'Stop being a factor' is a perfectly clinical, Abed-specific phrase. High quotability, genuine wit, and only Abed could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? Everyone gets extra credit. All of you. I'm just going to... I'm going to give it to you now before Garrett even starts, because I have no idea what's about to happen, and I'm not confident in my ability to encourage anything.

jokes.text: Jeff wrote 'LAW' on the board and his entire teaching ambition is to not erase it and 'maybe tomorrow we'll get even further'
jokes.setup: Jeff is ostensibly a law professor
jokes.punchline: His entire pedagogical progress is the word 'law' surviving on the board overnight — implying catastrophic laziness as an educator
jokes.explanation: Very Jeff — his staggering professional mediocrity compressed into one perfect image. The escalating ambition of 'maybe tomorrow we'll get even further' is a great button. Well integrated into his character's established laziness.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Garrett. Garrett Lambert. In case anyone was wondering, I'm the guy in the wheelchair.

jokes.text: Jeff gives everyone in class the extra credit because he's 'not sure how much I should encourage this'
jokes.setup: Garrett is about to present for extra credit
jokes.punchline: Jeff preemptively gives everyone the credit — telegraphing his anticipation that this will go badly — while framing it as beneficent uncertainty
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Jeff's low-grade dread of Garrett's presentation is funny, and the preemptive credit is a nice absurdist touch. Slightly undercut by being quickly superseded by the proposal.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I met Stacy at Pencils and Such. I was shopping for the such.

jokes.text: Garrett's PowerPoint slide reads 'This is me, Garrett. I'm in your class.' accompanied by what is presumably a photo of himself
jokes.setup: Garrett is doing a presentation on marriage law for extra credit
jokes.punchline: The presentation includes a slide formally introducing himself to people who have known him for years — with the unnecessary clarification that he is in the class
jokes.explanation: Garrett's oblivious sincerity shines here. The formal self-introduction to known classmates is perfectly pathetic in the best Garrett way. The redundancy of 'I'm in your class' as a clarifying detail is a gem.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: When I met Stacy, I thought I was experiencing romantic symptoms. My heart was racing, I couldn't sleep, I was constantly worried about what she thought of me.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Turns out those were just my baseline anxiety symptoms that actually improved when she was around.

jokes.text: The presentation is revealed to be an elaborate proposal — Garrett drops to one knee mid-class presentation
jokes.setup: Garrett's presentation is introduced as being about marriage law — audience and class expect a school report
jokes.punchline: It's a marriage proposal in front of the whole class, using the presentation format as the vehicle
jokes.explanation: Clean structural misdirection — 'marriage law' slides into 'this is Stacy, she is in our class as well' and then the proposal. The setup is tight and the reveal lands. Warmly funny rather than satirically sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm getting better at noticing faces.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's great, Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I still mostly use smell to tell people apart.

jokes.text: Garrett's description of meeting Stacy: 'I remember I was sweating a lot, and breathing heavy, and my heart felt like it was going to burst in my chest. But the day I met Stacy, most of those symptoms actually declined.'
jokes.setup: Garrett begins describing their first meeting with classic romantic symptoms — sweating, heavy breathing, heart pounding
jokes.punchline: These turn out to be his baseline medical state; Stacy's presence actually improved his condition
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes and among the best in the season. The setup perfectly mimics romantic confession tropes — the audience completes the expected arc — only for the punchline to reveal these are Garrett's normal symptoms. 'Most of those symptoms actually declined' is a clinical, devastating, and deeply funny subversion. It simultaneously characterizes Garrett's poor health AND his love story. The word 'declined' rather than 'disappeared' adds a layer of medical precision that makes it funnier. Near-perfect structure.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to go to the wedding alone and meet someone there. Statistically, weddings are one of the top five places to meet people. Right up there with work, college, and prison.

jokes.text: Jeff asks 'Are you quite done?' after witnessing the proposal — then is called out for having 'a strange look on your face'
jokes.setup: Jeff performs his standard detached sarcasm at the genuine romantic moment
jokes.punchline: Abed notices and calls out the face — implying Jeff's emotional suppression is visibly failing
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat — Abed's observational precision vs Jeff's emotional armor — but it's fairly standard territory for both characters and doesn't add a surprising twist.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: If you don't put that away right now, I'm going to stop loving you.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Happy birthday. Many happy returns.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Oh, you're noticing faces now? Aren't you still smelling hair to tell Frankie from Annie?'
jokes.setup: Jeff challenges Abed on 'noticing faces' as a new skill
jokes.punchline: Abed reveals Jeff's current workaround for distinguishing women is smelling their hair — a creepy and absurd character detail delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly specific character detail delivered with Abed's clinical neutrality. The idea that Jeff distinguishes women by scent rather than faces is both funny and mildly horrifying — and that Abed knows this and reports it without judgment is perfect. Strong originality, tight economy.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've already written a note explaining my disappearance. I've also pre-recorded a video of myself looking concerned, and I've arranged for someone to find one of my shoes by a river.

jokes.text: Jeff's reaction to the proposal: 'Well, it's official. I'm getting laid.'
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts emotionally to Garrett and Stacy's engagement
jokes.punchline: Jeff's emotional takeaway from witnessing true love is that he has identified an opportunity for himself
jokes.explanation: Very economical Jeff characterization — reduces a romantic moment to sexual opportunism in four words. Not groundbreaking but executed with perfect efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, the health department rejected returns on my kidney, so I guess I'm stuck with what I've got.

jokes.text: Annie filming herself as 'missing lover footage' — staging home-movie moments for a hypothetical future where she's been kidnapped or murdered
jokes.setup: Abed is filming Annie acting warmly and lovingly for the camera
jokes.punchline: The footage is explicitly for a 'hero' to watch in darkness after Annie is kidnapped or murdered — framed as proactive, healthy planning
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly dark concept — the trope of the dead/missing girlfriend's home footage deconstructed into something a character proactively prepares. 'Almost to the point of being stupid' as the aesthetic target is a great meta-joke on the trope itself. Abed-and-Annie collaboration makes this characterologically rich. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is Garrett. He's a student here at Greendale, and he's... well, he's visually distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I mean, he has a unique sense of style. His appearance is... memorable.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Oh, super healthy, guys.' Jeff: 'The health department called. They don't want anything back.'
jokes.setup: Britta sarcastically comments on the morbid murder-footage project
jokes.punchline: Jeff extends the health metaphor absurdly — the health department itself refuses to reclaim this behavior
jokes.explanation: Jeff's wordplay on Britta's 'healthy' riff is sharp — extending the metaphor into bureaucratic absurdity. Clean economy, good structure. The image of the health department declining to take something back is funny and original.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, we need exposition. Nobody knows what's happening.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the point. It's cinema verité.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It's cinema confusing. We need to explain things.

jokes.text: Britta describes Garrett as 'the funny-looking guy' in a confessional, then corrects to 'the eccentric-looking guy'
jokes.setup: Britta is asked to introduce Garrett for the documentary camera
jokes.punchline: She says 'funny-looking' on camera, is called out, and replaces it with a thesaurus-equivalent that is equally insulting
jokes.explanation: Classic Britta cringe — her self-correction is worse than the original. Functional and character-appropriate but fairly standard Britta territory.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're a tight-knit group of friends bound by an unbreakable bond forged in the crucible of higher education.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We would do anything for each other.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We're like family.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We literally just argued about who gets the good study table for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Annie and Britta argue about whether to clean or explain the cleaning for Abed's documentary — 'if we're both cleaning then there's nobody to explain why'
jokes.setup: Abed is filming their apartment preparation for the wedding
jokes.punchline: Annie is paralyzed by the documentary logic — if they're both performing the activity, there's no one to narrate it, which she treats as a genuine crisis
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-joke on documentary filmmaking conventions — the tension between doing and explaining what you're doing. Abed-adjacent humor that works because Annie has absorbed his meta-awareness. Good for genre-savvy Community fans.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, I see what's happening here. That sigh? That wasn't just about nail polish. You're expressing existential dread about the commodification of beauty standards in a patriarchal society.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I just couldn't decide between the two colors.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Exactly. The inability to choose reflects your deeper anxiety about identity and autonomy in a world that demands conformity.

jokes.text: Abed: 'She doesn't understand filmmaking.' Britta: 'I lived in New York.'
jokes.setup: Abed dismisses Britta's input on the documentary
jokes.punchline: Britta's rebuttal is 'I lived in New York' — offered as a complete and sufficient credential for filmmaking expertise
jokes.explanation: Perfect Britta economy. 'I lived in New York' as a complete argument is both character-specific (her pretentiousness) and structurally perfect — the non-sequitur logic delivered with full conviction. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I'm totally Jimming right now.

jokes.text: Annie and Britta describe themselves as 'an intensely, intimately bonded crew' in confessional — cut to screaming and chaos as they can't agree on nail color
jokes.setup: Confessional describes their friend group as profoundly bonded
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to screaming argument about nail polish color — classic mockumentary contradiction cut
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary ironic-cut joke — talking head claims one thing, action proves the opposite. Competent execution of a well-worn format beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I was talking to my accountant about it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your accountant?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I made it up. It's a figure of speech.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's not what a figure of speech is.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Well, it is to me. A figure of speech is when you lie.

jokes.text: Annie: 'That beleaguered sigh means, no, I can't have black nails.' Britta: 'You absolutely can, and we all will when our bodies decompose.'
jokes.setup: Britta sighs at Annie's request for black nail polish
jokes.punchline: Britta reframes the denial by pointing out that black is their inevitable future nail color — in death
jokes.explanation: Britta's nihilism channeled through nail polish is characterologically precise and genuinely funny. The image of post-mortem nail color as the ultimate resolution to the aesthetic argument is both dark and logically airtight — which makes it funnier. Good originality, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: The kind of person who says no to getting ready together is someone who doesn't want to share that moment. Someone who's socially awkward, maybe a little antisocial. Someone who would probably say no to a lot of things.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: But escalate that? That's the kind of person who commits biblical violence.

jokes.text: 'Please don't Jim the camera like that.' 'Jim the camera?'
jokes.setup: Annie objects to Abed's camera angle/reaction shot
jokes.punchline: She uses 'Jim' as a verb — referring to The Office's Jim Halpert looking at the camera — and Abed, the film expert, questions it
jokes.explanation: Exceptional meta-joke. 'Jim the camera' as a neologism — derived from Jim Halpert's signature Office camera looks — is clever, specific, and self-aware on multiple levels. It's a Community character critiquing the documentary format they're IN by reference to another show. That Abed doesn't recognize the term adds irony. Among the episode's most quotable and inventive lines.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: They threw rocks at me. Big rocks. Heavy rocks. Smooth rocks. Well-rounded rocks. Rocks with a certain je ne sais quoi. Rocks that had clearly thought about their life choices. Rocks that whispered secrets in the dead of night. Ninja rocks.

jokes.text: Argument about whether black is a color escalates — 'The color black hasn't had— It's not a color.' / 'I mean, absence of color.'
jokes.setup: Annie argues black nail polish is acceptable; Britta objects to the aesthetic
jokes.punchline: The argument devolves into whether black is technically a color — a pedantic derailment mid-fight
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation — the pivot into color theory is a decent derailment, but the joke runs a bit loose and doesn't quite pay off cleanly. Competent but not sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Frankie
dialogue.line: You know, I've been meaning to tell you guys something. My therapist says I have a tendency to overshare at inappropriate moments, which is probably why my last three relationships ended and also why I'm currently being investigated by the IRS.

jokes.text: 'My accountant has black nails!' / 'Your what?!' / 'Don't jump on that, my accountant, it's a figure of speech.' / 'It's a form of speech called making things up.'
jokes.setup: Britta cites her accountant as evidence that black nails are acceptable
jokes.punchline: Annie immediately clocks that Britta doesn't have an accountant; Britta's defense ('figure of speech') is exposed as improvised nonsense
jokes.explanation: Annie's 'It's a form of speech called making things up' is a sharp, precise comeback. The beat where Britta's poverty/disorganization is exposed by an accidental flex is very character-specific. Great structure — setup, escalation, devastating button.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We're not in a hurry. I batted the time.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know, like when you bat something away? I batted the time away.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: That's not a real phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It is now. I just invented it. When you bat the time, it means you have plenty of it.

jokes.text: Frankie's confessional: 'I didn't say no. Who says no to something like that? A cold, off-putting incompatible person.'
jokes.setup: Frankie explains why she agreed to come get ready with Annie and Britta
jokes.punchline: She answers her own rhetorical question by perfectly describing herself, with zero self-awareness that she's the answer
jokes.explanation: Clean self-own joke — Frankie defines the kind of person who would refuse, perfectly describing herself without recognizing it. Deadpan delivery is essential. Nice economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You see, what we have here is a delicate ecosystem of mutual reliance and interconnected success metrics.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's codependence.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, no, no. It's synergistic interdependence with a focus on integrated stakeholder outcomes.

jokes.text: Frankie: 'The kind of person that turns a sleepover into a stoning. I had rocks thrown at me. Biblical, igneous, jagged, hateful, pointy, ninja rocks, and that's not gonna happen again.'
jokes.setup: Frankie explains her motivation to participate in social activities
jokes.punchline: She reveals a past sleepover ended in her being literally stoned — and the escalating adjectives for the rocks ('biblical, igneous, jagged, hateful, pointy, ninja') reveal both trauma and a cataloguing mind
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best Frankie character moments. The pivot from metaphorical 'stoning' to literal rock-throwing is a perfect double-meaning payoff. But the genius is the escalating adjective list — 'biblical, igneous, jagged, hateful, pointy, ninja rocks' — which is simultaneously funny as a list, characterizes Frankie's precise/cataloguing nature, deepens the absurdity, and ends with 'ninja' as a perfect non-sequitur capstone. Exceptional originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, that's exactly what Annie said.

jokes.text: Annie and Frankie's small-talk loop — 'What have you been up to?' / 'I think you already asked that.' / 'Did you answer?' — neither can confirm what happened
jokes.setup: Annie and Frankie attempt to make small talk while getting ready
jokes.punchline: Their conversation falls into recursive uncertainty about whether a question was asked and answered — neither woman can confirm basic conversational facts
jokes.explanation: Smart cringe comedy — the social incompatibility of these two characters expressed through a conversational infinite loop. Frankie's social awkwardness and Annie's over-accommodation collide. Might read funnier on screen than on paper.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We're marrying Garrett to celebrities!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is the worst game I've ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You're just jealous because Garrett's marrying someone hotter than Britta.

jokes.text: Frankie: 'One of my sisters as well, you know, one of them is deceased, and the other is mentally retarded.'
jokes.setup: Frankie volunteers personal family information during small talk, apparently in response to something Annie said about her own family
jokes.punchline: Frankie volunteers the information with the same flat tone used for mundane facts — the clinical deadpan around 'deceased' and 'mentally retarded' makes it jarring and funny simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Frankie's tonal flatness applied to devastating personal facts is classic character comedy — her inability to modulate for emotional content is the joke. The word choice ('mentally retarded' vs more contemporary language) adds a layer of Frankie's clinical/dated register.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm so proud of how well I'm managing my time today.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We still have three more hours!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait... we were supposed to be there three hours ago.

jokes.text: Annie and Britta's pre-party drinking game: 'Panty raid. When I say drink, you say now. Drink. Now.' — discovered to be making them late
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta appear to be getting ready efficiently
jokes.punchline: They've been doing a drinking game ('panty raid') in the apartment, making themselves late — the responsible one (Annie) and the irresponsible one (Britta) are equally complicit
jokes.explanation: Functional reveal — the responsible women were day-drinking — but the joke itself isn't especially sharp. It's more a plot mechanism than a great comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've been left home alone.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, Abed's here, but he's filming, so basically I'm alone.

jokes.text: 'We lied to you about the time.' 'You need people whose flaws feed into each other.' 'Co-dependence.' 'Synergy.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Britta reveal they gave Frankie a fake earlier time to compensate for her lateness
jokes.punchline: They reframe obvious co-dependence as 'synergy' — corporate wellness language applied to dysfunction
jokes.explanation: The 'co-dependence/synergy' swap is a sharp comment on how groups euphemize dysfunction. Good but not exceptional — the concept is familiar from the show's ongoing theme of group dysfunction.

dialogue.speaker: Wedding Officiant
dialogue.line: You know, choosing a belief system is like choosing a life partner. You commit to it, you work through the hard times, and sometimes you realize it's not right for you. But what if I told you... what if I told you that you don't have to choose at all? What if the belief system chooses you? What if... what if I'm God?

jokes.text: Annie definition of synergy: 'there might be something that Annie hates doing, but she does it anyways, because what she really loves is to feel useful'
jokes.setup: Annie explains the group's synergy through examples
jokes.punchline: She accidentally describes her own compulsive helpfulness in the third person as evidence of synergy — not realizing she's pathologizing herself
jokes.explanation: Annie's self-analysis in the third person, presented as a compliment but functioning as a diagnosis, is a strong character-comedy moment. Her total lack of awareness that she's describing a compulsion is precisely what makes this funny and a little sad.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I may look complete on the outside, but I'm incomplete without Stacy.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Hey! I heard that laugh. Yeah, you in the back. My appearance is not the joke here.

jokes.text: Britta: 'You literally just defined co-dependence.' [raises glass] 'Here's to synergy.'
jokes.setup: Annie's definition of synergy has just been exposed as co-dependence
jokes.punchline: Britta acknowledges the diagnosis, then toasts to 'synergy' anyway — accepting the dysfunction while maintaining the euphemism
jokes.explanation: Good button on the co-dependence exchange — the toast to 'synergy' after the admission is a clean ironic closer. Economical and character-appropriate for Britta's mix of self-awareness and self-destruction.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: You guys were louder during my vow than I was during my actual vow.

jokes.text: Celebrity Garrett Marriage game — 'Do you, Garrett, take Jack Nicholson to be your lawfully wedded wife? I do. I do, Johnny.'
jokes.setup: The women are playing games to pass time before the wedding
jokes.punchline: They've invented a game marrying Garrett to celebrities — with Garrett presumably played by one of them doing a Garrett impression, and 'I do, Johnny' being an inexplicable Jack Nicholson quote from The Shining
jokes.explanation: 'I do, Johnny' as the Garrett/Nicholson wedding response is a funny specific choice — mixing The Shining with a wedding ceremony. The game concept is delightfully absurd. Slightly loses points for being setup-dependent on knowing Nicholson's specific quote.

dialogue.speaker: Stacy
dialogue.line: ...and that's why I'll always love you.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Those aren't vows. Vows are promises you make to each other, not reasons why you love someone.

jokes.text: 'There's only Nicholson.' — when someone suggests other celebrities for the game
jokes.setup: The Celebrity Garrett Marriage game is established with Jack Nicholson
jokes.punchline: One player rules that only Nicholson counts — arbitrary game taxonomy delivered with absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: The absolutism of 'there's only Nicholson' — made-up rule for a made-up game, enforced with total conviction — is a great little absurdist beat. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: It's Garrett, not Barrett.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh, so now we're not even going to try? That's racist.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? All of you are racist. Every single one of you.

jokes.text: 'Do you, Garrett, take Aubrey Plaza to be your wife?' / [solemn 'I do'] / pause / 'Wait. What do you mean, three more hours?'
jokes.setup: The game continues; they're having fun with time to spare
jokes.punchline: Mid-game, someone finally does the math and realizes they're catastrophically late — the bubble of absurd fun popping
jokes.explanation: Good comic timing beat — the moment of dawning horror breaking through the fun. The 'Aubrey Plaza' name drop (a Community-adjacent actress) adds a layer. Structurally it's a clean panic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett's Mom
dialogue.line: You kids need to keep it down. Some of us are trying to work.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett's Mom
dialogue.line: This constant noise is really starting to get to me.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett's Mom
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to be a burden, but if this keeps up, I don't think I'll have a reason to stick around, if you know what I mean!

dialogue.speaker: Garrett's Mom
dialogue.line: Anyway, who wants cookies?

jokes.text: They realize they've been playing the game for hours and are now actually late to the wedding — 'We're late. Aah!'
jokes.setup: Everyone assumed they had plenty of time because they lied to Frankie about the time
jokes.punchline: The lie about time was compounded by their own time distortion — everyone forgot the actual time
jokes.explanation: Plot mechanics joke — the irony of the lie rebounding on them is satisfying structurally but not especially funny as a standalone comedic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know, the thing about group dynamics is that they're fundamentally about power structures and social hierarchies. It's all very predictable once you understand the narrative framework we're operating in. But if you don't get that, that's your problem, not mine.

jokes.text: Chang is left behind: 'They left me home alone. I'm home alone. Well, not really.'
jokes.setup: Everyone rushes to the car; it becomes clear Chang has been abandoned
jokes.punchline: Chang's sad confessional — 'I'm home alone' — followed by his deflating self-correction 'Well, not really' suggesting he has company somehow, but that's even sadder
jokes.explanation: Chang's marginal status in the group is a consistent running gag. 'Well, not really' is a good button — but doesn't tell us what 'not really' means, which is funnier left ambiguous.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Elroy Patashnik. I'm a former IT professional turned instructor. I've been clean for three years now.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: But I'll be honest with you - I'm addicted to encouragement. I need it like some people need... well, like I needed other things.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Every morning I wake up and I think, 'Today's the day I stop needing positive reinforcement.' But by lunch, I'm jonesing for a compliment. By dinner, I'm mainlining affirmations.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: The worst part? Nobody understands. They think I'm just being positive. But this is serious. This is a disease.

jokes.text: The officiant's existential crisis about deity: 'What if I'm capable of total contradiction? What if science and religion were mine to wield as I choose? What if I'm God?'
jokes.setup: Wedding officiant begins the ceremony with a standard 'in the eyes of whatever power you choose' opening
jokes.punchline: He derails into a personal theological meditation, eventually positing that he himself might be God — in front of a waiting wedding congregation
jokes.explanation: The officiant's digression is a good absurdist character bit — the specific escalation from 'you choose your deity' to 'what if I'm God' is well-structured. The beat where he walks it back ('It is likely that I am not') adds a nice hedge that makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: I have a confession to make. I'm addicted to encouraging white people.

jokes.text: Officiant: 'It is likely that I am not [God], but I think it's totally out of line to take that possibility off of the table.'
jokes.setup: The officiant has just floated the possibility that he is God
jokes.punchline: The hedging walk-back — 'it is likely that I am not' — takes the metaphysical seriously with bureaucratic probability language
jokes.explanation: The 'likely that I am not' is a perfect button — probabilistic modesty applied to the question of personal divinity. 'Out of line to take that possibility off the table' is a great corporate-speak phrase for a theological claim.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Now, I'm not trying to be racist, but I've noticed something about Black people...

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Y'all are really resilient. Like, you survive everything. You're like the cockroaches of the human race, but in an inspirational way.

jokes.text: Garrett's vow: 'I know I look pretty complete.' — referring to appearing physically/emotionally whole without her
jokes.setup: Garrett says Stacy makes him realize he is 'incomplete' without her
jokes.punchline: He immediately acknowledges that he understands this is counterintuitive given his apparent completeness — with complete self-awareness and zero irony
jokes.explanation: Garrett self-aware about his own comedic appearance in the middle of sincere wedding vows is both funny and weirdly touching. 'I know I look pretty complete' is a great Garrett-specific line — nobody else could or would say it.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: I was doing so good. I had it under control.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: But then I realized... I'm doing it right now. I'm encouraging someone. And I can't stop.

jokes.text: 'Somebody over there laughed at that the wrong way.'
jokes.setup: Garrett says 'I know I look pretty complete' and someone in the congregation laughs
jokes.punchline: Garrett calls out the laugh as being mean-spirited rather than appreciative — mid-vow — asserting his own interpretation of how laughter at him should land
jokes.explanation: Genuinely layered — Garrett calling out 'wrong' laughter mid-vow is meta (he's aware people laugh at him), character-specific (Garrett's dignity despite everything), and also implicates the audience watching the show. The distinction between acceptable and 'wrong' laughter at Garrett is philosophically interesting. Very good beat.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Is my helpfulness problematic?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like we're both holding a dragon, and depending on how we grip it, it could be a gift or a curse.

jokes.text: Garrett's vow: 'You are my favorite video game.'
jokes.setup: Garrett's vows are building to romantic declarations
jokes.punchline: 'You are my favorite video game' as a sincere expression of devotion — the highest compliment in Garrett's register
jokes.explanation: Perfect character economy — this is Garrett's highest possible compliment, delivered sincerely. The specificity of 'favorite video game' (not 'my life,' not 'my dream') tells us everything about him in one phrase. Warm rather than mean.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Getting rid of helping others makes you selfish like Jeff.

jokes.text: The group's reaction noise is louder than Garrett's vow: 'Your [reaction] was louder than what I said.'
jokes.setup: Garrett says 'you are my favorite video game' and the group reacts enthusiastically in the middle of the ceremony
jokes.punchline: Garrett has to call them out for upstaging his own vows with their reaction
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — the group making themselves the center of attention at someone else's wedding is established here before it's later addressed by Garrett's mom. Functional but not outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Okay, we've got Puff the Magic Dragon, obviously. Then there's Smaug Connery, Khaleesi West, Drogon Dork—wait, that one doesn't work. Um, Drogoff Schwarzenegger, Falcor Schwarzenegger, Draco... Draco... okay I'm just saying celebrity names now.

jokes.text: Jeff welcomes the group barging through the bushes mid-ceremony: 'Everyone back there, you're welcome. Please join us. Any of those people could be God.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives late, crashing through a bush into the ceremony
jokes.punchline: The officiant, still in his God mode, welcomes them and suggests any of them could be God — completing the theological callback from his earlier digression
jokes.explanation: Clean callback to the God digression — his willingness to extend the theological possibility to late-arriving bush-crashers is funny and consistent with his established character. The structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Bones
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, HEY! What's up everybody! The party just got REAL!

dialogue.speaker: Bones
dialogue.line: Who wants to party with Bones? Come on!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh no.

dialogue.speaker: Bones
dialogue.line: You think you're better than me? You think you're SMARTER than me?

dialogue.speaker: Bones
dialogue.line: I'll fight every single one of you right now!

jokes.text: Stacy's vows: 'I love giving you your pain killers, at the end of the day.'
jokes.setup: Stacy's vows are a list of things she loves doing with Garrett — 'I love making sandwiches with you, I love folding towels with you'
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from domestic tenderness to 'I love giving you your pain killers' — implying Garrett has significant chronic pain, delivered with equal warmth
jokes.explanation: Perfectly integrates with the established Garrett-is-not-well theme (the symptoms joke earlier). The painkiller detail told with the same warm tone as 'I love folding towels' creates a great dark-subversive effect. Good escalation within the list.

dialogue.line: I cannot accurately parse this joke without the actual text of the punchline. Please provide the specific dialogue/joke text so I can identify the correct speaker(s) from the Community cast and reconstruct the speaker-attributed dialogue.

jokes.text: Officiant: 'Well, those aren't really vows. That's a list of things you love about me.' — catches himself — 'about Garrett, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Officiant notes that Stacy's vows are technically a list rather than promises
jokes.punchline: He says 'love about me' before correcting to 'about Garrett' — implying he momentarily inserted himself
jokes.explanation: The officiant continues to be a great character — his slip into first person during the vows is a good subtle character beat suggesting he's emotionally involved or just bizarre.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That toast was terrible. I've heard better speeches from a fire hydrant.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Here, let me show you how it's done. To the happy couple - may your love be as strong as my jawline and twice as symmetrical. Also, never trust a man in a turtleneck.

jokes.text: 'Where the party at?' / 'Okay, let's endure this.'
jokes.setup: The ceremony has just concluded and the reception begins
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response to 'where the party at' is 'let's endure this' — framing a joyful wedding reception as a trial to survive
jokes.explanation: Economical Jeff misanthropy. 'Endure' is the right word choice — not 'survive' or 'get through' but specifically 'endure' as if it's suffering. Character-consistent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I predict their marriage will fail by June, just like all my students.

jokes.text: 'Who would have thought Barrett's wedding would be the best day of our lives.' 'Definitely not Garrett, since his name's not Barrett.'
jokes.setup: A guest makes an enthusiastic toast mispronouncing the groom's name
jokes.punchline: The name correction lands as the punchline — particularly because the guest made such an emphatic statement about it being 'the best day'
jokes.explanation: Functional gag — the name correction as punchline is clean but fairly predictable. The 'definitely not Garrett' framing adds a mild twist.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Andi, you're not allowed to drink anymore. You're not allowed to go out on weekends. You're not allowed to talk to boys. You're not allowed to leave the house. You're not allowed to exist.

jokes.text: 'Racist.' 'Oh, no. You a racist.' 'That guy's a racist.' 'From here to there is racist.'
jokes.setup: Someone mispronounces the groom's name at a wedding with a Black guest present
jokes.punchline: The racism accusation spreads geometrically and illogically — eventually extending to the physical space between two people
jokes.explanation: 'From here to there is racist' is the best escalation beat here — the abstraction of racism from person to spatial relationship is a good absurdist escalation. The sequence is funny but belongs to background characters with no context.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you're both... the same person?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, that certainly explains why your family is so much closer than most.

jokes.text: Garrett's mom confronts the group: 'You came to a wedding in the middle of the vows through a bush.'
jokes.setup: The group has been behaving badly at the wedding
jokes.punchline: Garrett's mom delivers a simple factual recap of their behavior — through a bush, during vows — with devastating precision
jokes.explanation: The factual flatness of this indictment is excellent — no editorializing, just the specific details arranged for maximum shame. 'Through a bush' is a perfect final detail. High economy score for packing the entire group's embarrassment into one crisp sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Elroy
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! That's love right there. You married your cousin? That's beautiful, man. That's beautiful. Love is love.

jokes.text: 'I'm not Dr. Phil, but I don't want my son to kill himself, so do what you gotta do.'
jokes.setup: Garrett's mom is giving the group a reality check about their behavior
jokes.punchline: She pivots to dark self-interest — she doesn't want Garrett to kill himself, so she's pragmatically tolerating these people — delivered with cheerful passive-aggression
jokes.explanation: The 'don't want my son to kill himself' as the reason for tolerating the group is a great dark pivot — it contextualizes Garrett's existential fragility and her weary pragmatism simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is, Britta? You compare everything to Hitler. 'Oh, that's like Hitler.' 'Oh, that's basically the Holocaust.' You've made Hitler the control group for all of human behavior.

jokes.text: Jeff's confessional: 'The first piece I picked up was my own pride, all of it. It's almost like groups and people in groups, can never be complete at the same time. Does that make any sense? No? Well, that's your problem.'
jokes.setup: Jeff reflects on the group being humbled by Garrett's mom
jokes.punchline: His profundity about groups being incomplete dissolves into 'No? Well, that's your problem' — reabsorbing the humility back into arrogance mid-insight
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff structure — genuine insight followed immediately by defensive arrogance. 'That's your problem' as the button after a moment of apparent vulnerability is well-timed and perfectly in character. Good structure, high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Britta, you invoke Hitler way too much. It's like your default reference point.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's not fair. I hardly ever—you're just like Hitler!

jokes.text: Elroy's confessional: 'From 2006 to 2009, I was addicted to encouraging white people.'
jokes.setup: Elroy is at a wedding trying to be a good guest
jokes.punchline: He frames his ability to network at weddings as a former addiction — structured like an AA confession — specifically for encouraging white people
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best setups. The AA framing ('I was addicted') applied to the specific, socially astute behavior of encouraging white people is both sharp social comedy and excellent Elroy characterization. 'From 2006 to 2009' gives it the specificity of a real recovery narrative. High originality, great economy, distinctly his character.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? Love is love. Who are we to judge? If two people care about each other, that's what matters. And if we're talking about fault here, well, whose fault is it really? Is it their fault for loving each other, or is it society's fault for telling them they can't?

jokes.text: Elroy: 'White people like encouragement. It really doesn't matter what for.' / 'Now, that's a container for liquid.'
jokes.setup: Elroy explains the 'cheat code' for social success in white tech spaces
jokes.punchline: 'That's a container for liquid' as a demonstration — praising someone for holding a cup — proves the thesis that the content of encouragement is irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. 'That's a container for liquid' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode — the most reductive possible 'compliment' used to prove that white people respond to any encouragement regardless of content. The demonstration within the explanation is a brilliant structural choice. High on all axes.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We should stay together. We're a family.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I propose we do exactly that. All in favor?

jokes.text: Elroy (coaching himself in flashback): 'Oh, you know, you know what you're doing. This man knows exactly what he's doing.'
jokes.setup: Elroy explains he learned the 'cheat code' — white people like encouragement
jokes.punchline: His examples of encouragement are content-free affirmations that apply to anyone doing anything
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation of the 'encouragement' concept — the vacuousness of the praise is the joke, and each example shows him getting better at saying nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: This is MY wedding, and we're doing things MY way. You want cake? FINE. But you're going to ENJOY that cake, and you're going to smile while you eat it, or you're going straight to hell.

jokes.text: Elroy: 'I never felt like a sellout. I never laugh at anything unfunny, never said anything untrue. The thing is, and this will sound racist, white people are very discouraged, and very discouraging to each other.'
jokes.setup: Elroy is explaining the ethics and mechanics of his encouragement practice
jokes.punchline: 'This will sound racist' as a preface to what is actually a fairly compassionate observation — subverting the expected content of a 'this will sound racist' disclaimer
jokes.explanation: Smart social comedy — the 'this will sound racist' preface leads to what is actually an empathetic observation rather than a slur or stereotype. The subversion of expectation plus the genuine truth of the observation makes this land well. Elroy's perspective is specific and his voice is distinctive.

dialogue.speaker: Briggs Haddon
dialogue.line: You know, I was reading the newspaper this morning, and I came across the most fascinating quote defending cousin marriage. It was oddly specific—the kind of thing you don't expect to see in print.

jokes.text: Elroy: 'The thing is, and this will sound racist, white people are very discouraged, and very discouraging to each other.'
jokes.setup: 'This will sound racist'
jokes.punchline: The 'racist' statement is actually a compassionate observation about white social dynamics — funnier because it's both true and not what you expected from that qualifier
jokes.explanation: The 'this will sound racist' setup primes for offense, but the punchline is a surprisingly generous sociological observation. The subversion of the racist-warning trope is elegant and the observation itself has genuine insight. Strong originality and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Briggs Haddon
dialogue.line: You know, the inconsistency in interstate incest laws is really quite troubling. I actually had a personal experience with this.

dialogue.speaker: Briggs Haddon
dialogue.line: My cousin and I were legal in Nevada, but the moment we crossed into California, we were breaking the law.

jokes.text: Live demonstration: 'Sweetie, you're getting meatball juice everywhere but your plate.' / 'I think I'm going better than you are, with your asparagus.' / 'Oh, now that's the way to handle meatballs. And look at you. Working that asparagus.'
jokes.setup: Elroy is demonstrating his encouragement addiction relapsing in real time
jokes.punchline: He praises the same people whose food criticism he just witnessed — 'working that asparagus' transforms inept eating into triumph
jokes.explanation: 'Working that asparagus' is a great specific phrase — the gap between the mundane act (eating asparagus) and the encouraging language is exactly what the setup promised. The relapse structure is well executed. Good callback.

jokes.text: Elroy's addiction relapse: praising someone's pants so excessively he has to narrate himself — 'Oh look at these pants. Oh oh oh. He should keep on wearing, keep on wearing his pants. There's no lid.'
jokes.setup: Elroy is describing the danger of his encouragement addiction — 'if you don't put a lid on it'
jokes.punchline: He immediately loses control, praising a stranger's pants in real time, narrating his own relapse with 'there's no lid' — the metaphor becomes literal
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structure — 'if you don't put a lid on it' as the metaphor immediately paid off by 'there's no lid' as he spirals. The specific choice of pants — the most neutral possible garment — as the trigger for the relapse is perfect. 'He should keep on wearing, keep on wearing his pants' is a genuinely hilarious escalation. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Annie pushes someone she thinks is meemaw around the dance floor — it turns out to be Great Aunt Polly, Garrett's side
jokes.setup: Annie acts helpfully by dancing with what she assumes is Stacy's 90-year-old meemaw
jokes.punchline: She's pushing around the wrong 90-year-old — a stranger from the other family
jokes.explanation: Functional plot/comedy beat — Annie's compulsive helpfulness leads to an error. The setup is clean but the joke itself is thin; its importance is as a seed for the later twist. Gets a rewatch bonus for planting the same-town reveal.

jokes.text: Jeff to Annie: 'The world will still need you after you finish your cake.'
jokes.setup: Annie is about to rush off again on another helping mission
jokes.punchline: Jeff diagnoses her compulsion in one line — the world's need for her is not so urgent that she can't finish dessert
jokes.explanation: Very economical — implicitly calling out Annie's messiah complex while also just being a friend. The cake specificity makes it funnier than a generic 'slow down.' Jeff's warmth-through-sarcasm register is perfect here.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'We have the same dragon. Eventually you will slay it, or train it, or dissolve in its stomach. Its name is Helping Others.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is giving Annie advice about her compulsive need to help
jokes.punchline: He extends the dragon metaphor to include 'dissolve in its stomach' as a third option — which is not an inspiring outcome — and names the dragon 'Helping Others'
jokes.explanation: Jeff's dragon metaphor is excellent Community writing — it starts as a standard 'slay it or tame it' idiom but 'dissolve in its stomach' adds a third, nihilistic outcome that's both funny and honest. 'Its name is Helping Others' is a great specific naming that makes it feel like a real dragon. Strong across all metrics.

jokes.text: Annie: 'If I train it, can I give it a cooler name?' Jeff: 'If you train it, you can do anything you want. If you slay it, I don't know. I guess you get a new dragon named Yourself.'
jokes.setup: Annie asks about renaming the Helping Others dragon
jokes.punchline: Jeff extends the metaphor — slaying the dragon of altruism gets you a new dragon named 'Yourself' — the more terrifying dragon of self-focus, implicitly describing his own situation
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback and extension. 'A new dragon named Yourself' is both funny and cutting — slaying the altruism dragon leaves you with the narcissism dragon, which is what Jeff has. 'And then you'd be Jeff Winger' as the button is perfect. This is some of the best writing in the episode — the metaphor is internally consistent, character-specific, and genuinely insightful while being funny.

jokes.text: 'And then you'd be Jeff Winger.' / 'Yeah, that guy needs help!'
jokes.setup: Jeff says slaying the helping dragon gives you a dragon named 'Yourself'
jokes.punchline: Annie names Jeff explicitly, and Jeff agrees — 'that guy needs help' — in third person, with self-deprecating distance
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the dragon sequence. Jeff's third-person self-deprecation — 'that guy needs help' about himself — is funny, honest, and character-precise. The willingness to admit it while maintaining one degree of remove is exactly Jeff.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Is what I wanted to say, but how is that my business?' — after suggesting Jeff needs to get away from his influence
jokes.setup: Annie is thinking about telling Jeff something important about her future
jokes.punchline: She narrates her own decision NOT to say something — mid-sentence — stopping herself in real-time and questioning her own impulse to intervene
jokes.explanation: Annie's self-interruption — beginning the advice, stopping, questioning her jurisdiction — is a subtle but effective beat about her character growth. The meta-narration of stopping herself is unusual and character-specific.

jokes.text: Annie shows Jeff her dragon name list — she doesn't show people when she finishes them. 'So then why do you make them, again?' / 'It relaxes me. It's like knitting with less discipline.'
jokes.setup: Annie shows Jeff a list she's been making at the reception
jokes.punchline: 'It's like knitting with less discipline' — reframing list-making as a hobby/vice with its own craft hierarchy
jokes.explanation: 'Like knitting with less discipline' is a highly quotable, specifically Annie-flavored description of list-making. The implication that knitting is the disciplined version of her compulsion is funny and character-precise. High economy.

jokes.text: Annie's dragon name list: 'Princess Firebreath. Sir Pent. Doctor Rachel Spinetail. Holly Hotbreath. Jimmy Talon. Christian Scale. Carson Scaley. Jude Claw. Ariana Puffington.' — 'I got into a bit of a celebrity pun barrel here.'
jokes.setup: Annie is making a list of dragon names; it starts with original names
jokes.punchline: The list devolves into celebrity puns (Sir Pent, Jude Claw, Ariana Puffington) — with Annie's self-aware comment 'I got into a bit of a celebrity pun barrel'
jokes.explanation: The pun list is good — 'Sir Pent' and 'Jude Claw' are strong entries, 'Ariana Puffington' is a great capstone. 'Celebrity pun barrel' as her self-diagnosis is a great Annie phrase. The escalation from genuine to pun-dependent is well-structured.

jokes.text: 'Garrett's older brother Bones has relapsed during his weekend pass and will be unable to do the best man toast.'
jokes.setup: Jeff explains why he's giving the best man toast instead
jokes.punchline: 'Weekend pass' and 'relapsed' — mentioned with the same matter-of-fact tone as any other logistical update — implies the brother is in some kind of facility and has relapsed during supervised release
jokes.explanation: Classic Community dark-subversive — massive negative life event delivered as logistics. The specificity of 'weekend pass' implying institutional supervision is a good dark detail. Economy is high because the detail is packed into one phrase.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm not gonna Winger speech it, this is a thing of substance.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is preparing to give a genuinely good toast rather than his usual manipulative rhetoric
jokes.punchline: He invents 'Winger speech' as a verb — referring to his own signature move as a known, nameable thing that he is consciously choosing not to do
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-character moment — 'Winger speech it' as a self-referential verb is a great piece of Community self-awareness. Jeff naming his own trope and declaring he won't use it is both funny and meaningful. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'This wedding is gonna regret the day it thought we'd make it about us.'
jokes.setup: Jeff rallies the group to redeem themselves as wedding guests
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'this wedding is gonna regret' anthropomorphizes the wedding as an adversary — framing selfless behavior as a competitive victory they will inflict on the event
jokes.explanation: Very Jeff — the good behavior is reframed as winning against a personified wedding. His inability to frame selflessness as anything other than a competition is precisely his character's pathology. Good line.

jokes.text: 'God, I love my job! Wait, this isn't my job. God, I love myself!'
jokes.setup: Jeff is in full speech-preparation mode, feeling good about the toast
jokes.punchline: He catches his professional instinct mid-sentence and replaces it with pure narcissism — 'I love myself' as the accurate correction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable moments. The self-correction from 'my job' to 'myself' is a perfect Jeff beat — the precision of identifying 'this isn't my job' makes the narcissism more conscious and therefore funnier. Extremely high economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Bad toast example: 'That was Stacy's first time! But it's not gonna be her last time, right Garrett?'
jokes.setup: Stacy's friend Andi is giving a terrible toast before Jeff
jokes.punchline: Andi's toast implies Garrett will be responsible for ensuring Stacy has future 'first times' — a toast that's inexplicably salacious or nonsensical at a wedding
jokes.explanation: The bad toast jokes serve the narrative (setting up Jeff's redemptive toast) more than landing as great comedy in themselves. This one is functional cringe.

jokes.text: 'So many classic toast errors. A fire hydrant could follow this.'
jokes.setup: Andi's terrible toast has just concluded
jokes.punchline: 'A fire hydrant could follow this' — the bar has been set so low that an inanimate object would be an improvement
jokes.explanation: Very economical and quotable. The specificity of 'fire hydrant' (not 'anything', not 'an object' — a fire hydrant, which is both mute and outside) is exactly the right image. Jeff's confidence is fully intact going into his toast.

jokes.text: Andi's toast: 'I love you so much, and please, keep painting. Don't let Garrett, don't paint. Don't let Garrett keep you from painting.'
jokes.setup: Andi's toast continues to unspool
jokes.punchline: She gets tangled in her own phrasing, nearly advising Stacy not to let Garrett paint (implying he'd be a threat to it), then corrects — but the correction is equally confused
jokes.explanation: The tangled phrasing is a decent cringe moment — the speech deteriorating into self-contradiction is effective. Gains points for the specificity of 'painting' as the high-stakes topic.

jokes.text: Jeff's toast opener: 'There's a lot of things I can say about this couple. They're both in my class at Greendale, and like all my students, I give them till about June.'
jokes.setup: Jeff begins the best man toast with a standard 'things I can say about this couple' opener
jokes.punchline: 'I give them till about June' — framing the marriage through his teacher-giving-up-on-students lens — before immediately walking it back
jokes.explanation: Excellent toast opener — merging his teacher cynicism with his wedding-guest role. 'I give them till about June' is funny on its own and also perfectly inverts the toast form (should be optimistic). The callback to his terrible teaching established in the opening scene is a good structural bonus.

jokes.text: Jeff continues: 'No, you guys'll be fine forever, as long as Stacy never lets Andi babysit. Or go near a child. Or be in the same town as a pair of scissors. This girl's a wreck.'
jokes.setup: Jeff pivots from his negative opening to a positive statement about the couple — 'you'll be fine forever'
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts it with an escalating list of conditions that require keeping Andi away from children and scissors — roasting the previous bad-toast-giver in real time
jokes.explanation: Solid escalating roast — 'scissors' is the perfect final specific detail. The escalation from 'babysit' to 'near a child' to 'same town as scissors' builds well. The callback to Andi's visible terribleness pays off. Jeff reading the room and roasting the problem element is very true to character.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'you guys'll be fine forever, as long as Stacy never lets Andi babysit. Or go near a child. Or be in the same town as a pair of scissors. This girl's a wreck.'
jokes.setup: Jeff corrects himself — they'll be fine — but conditions it
jokes.punchline: The conditions escalate from 'babysit' to 'scissors' — each step more absurd, suggesting Andi is a danger to society
jokes.explanation: Good escalation joke. The progression from babysitting restrictions to scissors proximity is well-paced. 'This girl's a wreck' as a plain-spoken button is effective.

jokes.text: Guest reactions to Jeff's toast: 'He's being too mean.' / 'No, he's reading the room.' / 'Andi was a bummer, they needed this.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is roasting Andi during the wedding toast
jokes.punchline: The wedding guests debate the ethics of his roast in real time — the meta-commentary on toast etiquette played as comedy
jokes.explanation: Functional commentary — the guest debate about toast ethics is a nice observational beat. 'Andi was a bummer, they needed this' is the best line of the three. Not exceptional but good texture.

jokes.text: Jeff reveals that meemaw and Aunt Polly appear to be the same person — 'I feel like an idiot' — and delivers the punchline: 'either someone here is lying, or this family's a lot closer than we thought'
jokes.setup: Jeff's toast has been building to a touching moment connecting the two families through two 90-year-old women from the same town
jokes.punchline: The grand reveal collapses — meemaw and Aunt Polly appear to be the same person, meaning Garrett and Stacy may be cousins
jokes.explanation: The episode's central twist and best structural joke. The entire toast — the mingling, the networking, the warm revelation — builds to this devastating inversion. 'This family's a lot closer than we thought' is perfect deadpan understatement for the reveal that they're cousins. The craft is in the long setup (starting from 15:21 with the wrong grandmother) paid off here. Excellent earned-not-cheap scoring.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Garrett, where's Aunt Polly?' — nobody can produce Aunt Polly because Polly and Meemaw are the same person
jokes.setup: Jeff calls for both women to come forward
jokes.punchline: Polly can't be located because she IS meemaw — the families share the same elderly woman, implying familial overlap
jokes.explanation: The incest reveal landing moment. The structure is impeccable — the audience gets there just before Jeff does, and the gap is perfect. High structural craft and enormous impact in the room.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I now don't feel as stupid because either someone here is lying, or this family's a lot closer than we thought.'
jokes.setup: Polly can't be found; Annie's meemaw IS Polly
jokes.punchline: Jeff processes the logical consequence ('this family's a lot closer than we thought') with professional calm — the understatement of 'a lot closer' for incest is perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'This family's a lot closer than we thought' as a euphemism for cousin incest is brilliantly understated. Jeff's ability to maintain composure while delivering this bombshell is in perfect character. Very quotable.

jokes.text: 'And now, this is a man that knows how to marry his cousin.'
jokes.setup: The revelation that Garrett and Stacy may be cousins has just landed
jokes.punchline: The officiant responds with flat, admiring endorsement — 'this is a man that knows how to marry his cousin' — with the same tone used for genuine compliments
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The officiant's unfazed, admiring tone — applied to cousin marriage — is perfect. The flatness of the delivery is essential. 'Knows how to marry his cousin' as praise is absurdist and devastating. Extremely high economy — nine words that contain the entire joke. Among the most quotable lines.

jokes.text: Annie: 'None of this would have happened if I wasn't always trying to help.' Jeff: 'Actually, none of this would have happened if I hadn't tried helping you with your helpfulness.'
jokes.setup: The group reflects on how they ruined the wedding
jokes.punchline: Jeff meta-traces causality back through layers of helping — he caused this by helping Annie with her helping problem, which is itself a helping problem
jokes.explanation: Good callback — the layered causality of helping-about-helping is a solid comic beat that also genuinely reflects the episode's theme. The irony that Jeff's coaching made things worse is character-fitting.

jokes.text: Annie: 'None of us would have met if Hitler hadn't been born.' / 'Also none of Britta's arguments would have a default analogy.'
jokes.setup: Annie tries to extend the causal chain beyond Jeff's meta-blame
jokes.punchline: She invokes Hitler — revealing this is a go-to analogy for her — and Jeff immediately adds that Hitler is specifically Britta's rhetorical default
jokes.explanation: The 'Britta goes to Hitler' joke is a solid running character beat — her tendency to escalate arguments to Hitler comparisons has been established. The double-punchline (Annie reaches for Hitler; Jeff says Britta owns that well) is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Britta: 'What are you, Hitler, Hitler?' — in response to being accused of using Hitler analogies too much
jokes.setup: Jeff accuses Britta of overusing Hitler comparisons
jokes.punchline: Her defense is to immediately use Hitler as a comparison — 'what are you, Hitler, Hitler?' — proving his point in real time
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes and a genuinely elite sitcom line. Britta defending herself against the Hitler-analogy accusation by immediately invoking Hitler is structurally perfect — she proves the point in the most economical and ironic way possible. 'Hitler, Hitler' as a doubled formulation (what are you?) is both baffling and hilarious. Near-perfect on all axes. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Okay, Britta, we're all the worst right now, take a day off.' Britta: 'I did.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Britta to 'take a day off' from being the worst
jokes.punchline: 'I did' — Britta points out this is her day off, implying normal Britta is even worse
jokes.explanation: Brilliant economy — two words that completely flip the meaning of Jeff's command. 'I did' implies this disaster is Britta's relaxed mode, which is a perfect and devastating character point. One of the most economical jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Britta: 'Between us ruining the ceremony and ruining the reception, when we were all just individual people, I wasn't the worst. I'm only the worst with you guys.'
jokes.setup: Britta is defending herself from being called the worst
jokes.punchline: She makes the astute and slightly sad observation that the group brings out her worst — 'I'm only the worst with you guys' — framing group membership as her dysfunction trigger
jokes.explanation: Genuinely interesting character insight delivered as a complaint. 'I'm only the worst with you guys' is both funny and emotionally resonant — it's simultaneously a defense and an admission of belonging. Good for rewatch because it's a true statement about all of them.

jokes.text: Dean: 'I was a good dean before you guys. You can't disprove it.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is admitting the group brings out their worst
jokes.punchline: Dean's contribution is unfalsifiable — he was a good dean before — and his insistence that it 'can't be disproved' adds an epistemological desperation
jokes.explanation: 'You can't disprove it' as the coda is excellent — the defensive epistemology of someone whose good dean career is entirely theoretical (pre-dating all witnesses) is both funny and sad. Very Dean.

jokes.text: Elroy: 'I relapsed because of you guys.' / 'What? Oh it's not a big deal.' / 'White people problems.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing how the group brings out their dysfunction
jokes.punchline: Elroy blames them for his encouragement relapse; someone dismisses it as 'not a big deal'; Elroy delivers 'white people problems' — recontextualizing the dismissal as the exact white-people-discouraging-each-other behavior he described
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback structure. Elroy's 'white people problems' is a perfect button — it both dismisses the dismissal AND directly demonstrates the thesis from his confessional (white people are discouraging to each other). The person saying 'it's not a big deal' is precisely the behavior Elroy described. Triple-layered payoff: callback, character moment, and sociological point. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: 'I like this group. I'm at my best when I'm with you guys.' / 'Well, that clinches it. Separate cabs.'
jokes.setup: Someone (likely a minor character or Garrett) expresses genuine warmth about the group
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate response to 'I'm at my best with you guys' is 'separate cabs' — the warm sentiment acting as the trigger for dispersal
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Jeff line. 'Separate cabs' as the response to genuine warmth is a great character-defining moment — his reflexive retreat from sentimentality, compressed into two words. Strong across all metrics. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Garrett announces from the stage that they won't be cutting the cake or dancing, and there was a Homer Simpson costume surprise that 'won't be necessary'
jokes.setup: Garrett addresses the reception following the cousin revelation
jokes.punchline: The list of cancelled wedding activities — including a Homer Simpson costume that was apparently going to be a surprise — is delivered with matter-of-fact resignation
jokes.explanation: The Homer Simpson costume is a perfect specific absurdist detail — unexplained, presented as though it's normal, and cancelled without explanation. The matter-of-fact cancellation of fun is sad-funny. Good Garrett specificity.

jokes.text: Chang's speech: 'Hey, screw you guys. No, this family is so screwed up, you thought you were two different families. Now that you know you're not, you can't wait to leave. For you? You want him to take one for this crappy team?'
jokes.setup: Everyone wants the wedding called off due to the cousin revelation
jokes.punchline: Chang, of all people, gives the most emotionally coherent speech of the night — the family is so dysfunctional they didn't know they were the same family, and NOW they're drawing a moral line
jokes.explanation: Chang's unexpected championing of the couple is played both as comedy and genuine character moment. The logic — 'you're mad that they're related, but you didn't know you were the same family' — is sharp. Good irony that the most marginal group member delivers the most sensible argument.

jokes.text: Jeff/Chang to congregation: 'Is anyone here going to make less fun of these two or be better friends to them no matter what they do?' / The congregation responds: 'No. No. No.'
jokes.setup: Jeff/Chang makes the case for the marriage by pointing out no one else will be better
jokes.punchline: The congregation honestly answers 'No' to whether they'll be better to Garrett and Stacy — the brutal truthfulness of the crowd makes the argument for the marriage
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny — the entire congregation honestly admitting they won't be better to Garrett and Stacy is both the punchline AND the logical argument for the marriage. The 'No. No. No.' chorus is a great absurdist-dark beat. High earned-vs-cheap because it's genuinely earned by the speech.

jokes.text: Garrett: 'Stacy, will you be my legally incestuous wife?'
jokes.setup: Garrett is re-proposing after the cousin revelation, in the spirit of Chang's argument
jokes.punchline: 'Legally incestuous' as the new framing for his proposal — Garrett makes the legal technicality part of the vow itself, with full ownership
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable lines. 'Legally incestuous' as a romantic term of commitment is brilliantly absurd — it's accurate, specific, and Garrett owns it completely. The callback to the original proposal structure gives it emotional resonance. Near-perfect economy and character integration. This is a genuinely exceptional TV joke.

jokes.text: Stacy: 'Yes.' / Garrett: 'Everyone stay and eat cake, or go to hell.'
jokes.setup: Stacy says yes to the re-proposal
jokes.punchline: Garrett's post-acceptance address to the guests: 'stay and eat cake, or go to hell' — a binary with equal hospitality and hostility
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode button line. The duality of 'stay and eat cake, or go to hell' — presenting hospitality and hostility as equivalent options — is brilliant. Garrett has earned this moment, and the casual delivery of 'go to hell' is completely unexpected from him. Near-perfect economy. Among the most quotable lines in the episode and possibly the season.

jokes.text: Abed talking-head: 'This is about me. I didn't think I could do it, but I did.'
jokes.setup: The wedding has resolved; everyone is reflecting
jokes.punchline: Abed's confessional is entirely self-referential about his filming — 'this is about me, I didn't think I could do it' — referring to the documentary itself, not Garrett's wedding, in a moment supposed to be about the couple
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — inserting himself as the subject of a moment meant to be about others, with complete sincerity. The flatness of 'this is about me' as the opening of an end-of-episode reflection is funny and character-perfect.

jokes.text: Post-credits meta-segment: 'Wow, what an episode of Community.' — writer Briggs Haddon appears on camera to defend the episode's incest content
jokes.setup: The episode appears to have ended; a new segment begins with someone complimenting the episode
jokes.punchline: The credited writer of the episode appears and identifies himself, claiming he has spent two years researching incest on the internet and inserted it into the episode for advocacy purposes
jokes.explanation: Exceptional meta-joke that only Community could do. The writer appearing post-credits to 'take credit' for incest advocacy is a brilliant subversion of the standard 'important message' PSA format. 'Researching incest on the internet' as a two-year project is darkly hilarious. The specific legal detail ('I can make love to my cousin in Nebraska but if I take her on a date in South Dakota, I'm looking at 15 years') adds perfect specificity. The condition for the segment ('I must appear and identify myself as a writer') is a great internal joke about how the network/showrunner handles writers going rogue. Very high originality.

jokes.text: Briggs: 'I can make love to my cousin in Nebraska, but if I take her on a date in South Dakota, I'm looking at 15 years prison time.'
jokes.setup: Briggs is making a legal argument for cousin marriage rights
jokes.punchline: His specific example — the Nebraska/South Dakota border creating a legal minefield for cousin dating — delivered with the gravity of a civil rights argument
jokes.explanation: The specific state-by-state legal detail delivered as genuine advocacy is very funny — the specificity of 15 years for a South Dakota date implies he's looked this up and treats it as urgent. 'Make love to my cousin' in the phrasing is an intentional archaic/formal register that adds absurdity.

jokes.text: Briggs: 'I told the Community writers, attention must be paid. They said they'd allow me to address it on one condition. At the end of the episode, I must appear and identify myself as a writer.'
jokes.setup: Briggs is explaining how he got permission to include the incest content
jokes.punchline: The 'condition' is hilariously mild — just that he identify himself — implying the writers room agreed to the content as long as this one guy takes personal responsibility
jokes.explanation: The 'condition' is the best part of the meta-joke — it implies the writers room negotiated exactly the kind of CYA arrangement real network TV uses, except the content is advocating cousin marriage. The specificity of 'identify myself as a writer' as the full condition is perfect. Strong originality and structure.

jokes.text: Briggs: 'Look, I'm not trying to tell you how to feel about incest, I'm just letting you know, there's more to it than you've been told. I'm Briggs Haddon, and I wrote the Community season six, incest episode. Good night.'
jokes.setup: Briggs wraps up his incest advocacy segment
jokes.punchline: 'I'm Briggs Haddon, and I wrote the Community season six, incest episode. Good night.' — the formal sign-off treats incest advocacy as equivalent to a news broadcast or public service announcement
jokes.explanation: 'I wrote the Community season six, incest episode. Good night.' is an all-time great episode button. The formal broadcast-sign-off register, combined with the specificity of 'incest episode,' and the finality of 'Good night' — it's perfectly structured absurdist comedy. Highly quotable and a memorable closer.

tmdb_overview: When two Greendale students get married, the wedding reception takes a turn after Jeff unwittingly exposes an inconvenient truth.
insight: Season 6's tonal pivot lands: character comedy sustains 85-point episode on escalation alone.
